description_full: Mechanics Bancorp operates as the holding company for Mechanics Bank that provides banking services in California, Oregon, Washington, and Hawaii.It offers various checking and savings accounts, retirement accounts, money market accounts, time certificates of deposit, and safe deposit boxes. The company also provides home loans, auto loans, term loans and lines of credit, owner occupied real estate lending services, small business lending loans, multi-family lending services; mortgage and consumer lending loans; commercial real estate loans; residential construction loans; private banking, such as loan program, personal lines of credit and investment management and trust lines of credit. In addition, it offers unsecured consumer installment loans and personal reserve accounts; automated bill payments, remote and mobile deposit capture, automated clearing house origination, wire transfer, lockbox, payee positive pay, and direct deposit; digital banking. Further, the company provides real estate, escrow services, title, labor unions, nonprofits and property management services. Mechanics Bancorp was founded in 1905 and is headquartered in Walnut Creek, California.

financial_summary: Mechanics Bancorp is a mid-cap financial services business with a $3.3B market cap on $809M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +42% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $187M in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.73× cash conversion.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 82% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sect: Its 40% operating margin runs 10pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.52x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+12.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 25% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.40 vs 5y 0.95), so read it loosely.
About $7.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash and 58% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 27% below its DCF fair value of $20.25, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 91%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.79 to $24.93 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 17.4 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 84% below its 10-year median.
The 4 covering analysts target $16.25 on average, 10% above the price.
The price implies 0.2% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.95).
It converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 9% return on equity.
Operating margin is running 37pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 41.6% over 3 years, 17.7% over 5 years and 6.5% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 261%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 30.8% on average.
Analysts expect 9.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 82.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 11%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.5% (10.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 101% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 10.1% of the float, 7.2 days to cover.
people: With about 1,768 employees, each generates about $457K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 8.0% a year.
That works out to $106K of free cash flow per employee.
